questions.q: Per this lesson, what is the single highest-impact performance habit taught across the entire course?
options: Never putting a SOQL query or DML statement inside a loop
Choosing descriptive variable names
Always using global access modifiers
Writing custom exceptions for every method
questions.explain: Bulkification — never issuing a query or DML statement inside a loop — is called out again here as the single highest-impact habit, consistent with its emphasis throughout Chapters 3 and 4.

questions.q: Why is `Set<Id>.contains()` a better choice than `List<Id>.contains()` for checking membership in a large collection?
options: List.contains() does not compile on collections larger than 200 elements
Set can only hold Id values, while List can hold any type
A List performs a linear scan for contains(), while a Set is the structure actually designed for efficient membership checks
There is no actual difference between the two
questions.explain: List.contains() scans the list entry by entry, while Set is specifically the collection type suited to fast membership checks — a performance difference rooted in choosing the right collection type, from Lesson 4.

questions.q: What is a `@future` method typically used for?
options: Running a method synchronously with guaranteed immediate completion
Declaring a class as an interface
Replacing the need for triggers entirely
Running a method asynchronously, useful for offloading something like an HTTP callout outside the main transaction
questions.explain: @future methods run asynchronously, which is useful for offloading work — like a callout not permitted in certain contexts — outside the main synchronous transaction.

questions.q: What advantage does Queueable Apex have over a `@future` method, per this lesson?
options: Queueable Apex has no governor limits at all
Queueable Apex supports richer parameter types (objects, not just primitives) and can be chained, with one job enqueueing another
Queueable Apex always runs synchronously
Queueable Apex cannot be used for callouts
questions.explain: Queueable Apex supports more complex parameter types than @future's primitive-only parameters, and supports chaining jobs together, which @future does not support.

questions.q: What does this lesson mean by treating performance as 'a design question, not a fix'?
options: Bulk behavior (how code performs at 200+ records, not just 1) should be considered while designing code, since retrofitting it later is far more expensive
Performance should only be considered after a production failure occurs
Performance doesn't matter for Apex code written for internal use only
Only Batch Apex jobs need to consider performance at design time
questions.explain: The lesson's closing habit is to ask how code will behave at real volume while designing it, since every pattern covered is cheap to apply from the start and expensive to retrofit after a feature already assumes the wrong scale.
